claims.text: Untreated W–Cu composites containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix are prone to phase separation under service conditions.
Untreated W–Cu composites are prone to interfacial void formation under service conditions.
An ultrathin refractory coating can be deposited on W surfaces before W–Cu composite fabrication, for example by physical vapor deposition.
The refractory coating can be applied uniformly to all W surfaces.
Joints between W-based plasma-facing components and Cu-based cooling components experience high thermal flux and irradiation.
The deposited interfacial coating creates a graded transition between W and Cu.
A refractory interlayer reduces the interfacial energy mismatch between W and Cu.
Reducing the W–Cu interfacial energy mismatch suppresses phase separation under thermal and irradiation stress.
Reducing the W–Cu interfacial energy mismatch suppresses nucleation of interfacial voids under thermal and irradiation stress.
Deposited interfacial coatings can enhance bonding relative to an uncoated composite.
Enhanced W–Cu interfacial bonding prevents defect formation under high heat flux and irradiation.
Interfacial defect formation decreases the thermal conductivity of W–Cu composites.
The coated W–Cu composite will exhibit less phase separation than the untreated composite after combined heat-flux and irradiation exposure.
The coated W–Cu composite will exhibit fewer interfacial voids than the untreated composite after combined heat-flux and irradiation exposure.
The coated W–Cu composite will have higher thermal conductivity than the untreated composite under combined high-heat-flux and irradiation conditions.
The intervention is applicable when a uniform, ultrathin refractory coating can be reliably deposited on W surfaces.
The coating is expected to remain effective under current plasma-facing and cooling-component operating conditions.
Performance at temperatures or irradiation levels far beyond current benchmarks is uncertain.
